Confirmed via git log -S 'def _require_auth' that the global auth interceptor landed in 5aa8ed6 (2026-09-13), i.e. before the baseline. No request was sent and no file was modified.

title: LAN knock client eval()s shell code generated from the JSON configuration file (command injection through config values)
description:
STATUS: FIXED in the current source (commit 31509ea, 2026-10-30, 'fix(v0.8.9): 面板侧 P1/P2 批量修复'). Kept so the reconciliation can confirm the baseline entry is closed.

The original mechanism: when no host/ports are given on the command line, the script had python print shell assignments such as HOST="..." / PORTS="..." and then eval'd them. The developers' own comment at setup/knock-lan.sh:62-68 preserves the original reasoning: the config file's router_ip4 is a USER-WRITTEN field, so a value carrying a quote and an embedded shell command would execute arbitrary commands inside the eval (setup/knock-lan.sh:62-68).

The current code has removed the eval entirely and the value never reaches a second shell parse:
  - The python helper now prints only PURE VALUES, one per line, and a charset filter keeps just alphanumerics plus . : _ - (setup/knock-lan.sh:76 and 82). The comment states the intent explicitly: the result must be data, not code.
  - The shell extracts them with sed into plain variables (setup/knock-lan.sh:99: HOST=$(printf '%s\n' "$CONFIG_VALS" | sed -n '1p')), which does not re-parse the content.
  - The old 'eval echo' port extraction is gone too: the ports are read with a plain case statement (setup/knock-lan.sh:188 onward).

REQUIRES: the knock client is a LOCAL script run by the operator on the LAN host, and the tainted field (router_ip4) is written by the router's own panel config. The attacker_position is therefore LOCAL and privileges_required is LOW (write access to that config file).
impact: None in the current code for this vector. Historically, a value written into the router config's router_ip4 field would be executed as a shell command on every LAN knock run.
mitigation: Already fixed (setup/knock-lan.sh:62-100). Keep the charset filter and the sed extraction, and add a regression test asserting that the script contains no eval of configuration-derived values.
verification: Read setup/knock-lan.sh end to end, in particular lines 54-100 (config reading), 130-150 (valid_host) and 155-200 (send_udp and port extraction); confirmed via git log -S 'P1-39' that the fix landed in commit 31509ea (2026-10-30). No script was executed and no file was modified.

title: LAN knock client injects the unvalidated host argument into a `bash -c` command string (shell command injection)
description:
STATUS: FIXED in the current source (commit 31509ea, 2026-10-30). Kept so the reconciliation can confirm the baseline entry is closed.

The original mechanism: the UDP knock was sent with a bash -c command string into which the host and port were interpolated directly. A host containing a semicolon or a command substitution was parsed as an extra command, and a host containing a slash could traverse the /dev/udp path prefix.

The current code has two independent fixes.
  - valid_host() (setup/knock-lan.sh:141) rejects any character outside [0-9A-Za-z.:_-] with the case pattern *[!0-9A-Za-z.:_-]*) return 1, and the script refuses to continue when it fails (setup/knock-lan.sh:149). The developers' comment at setup/knock-lan.sh:134-140 records the exact rationale: the host goes into a bash -c command string or into a /dev/udp path component.
  - The interpolation itself was removed. The call is now timeout 3 bash -c 'exec 3<>/dev/udp/"$1"/"$2" && printf "k" >&3' _ "$host" "$port" (setup/knock-lan.sh:171): the values are passed as POSITIONAL PARAMETERS and the command string only references "$1" and "$2", so they are never parsed as shell code. The comment at setup/knock-lan.sh:166-170 states this explicitly.
  - The ncat / nc fallbacks (setup/knock-lan.sh:173-177) pass the values as quoted arguments to a real binary, not through a command string.

REQUIRES: the knock client is a LOCAL script run by the operator on the LAN host; the tainted input is the same user-writable router_ip4 config field, or the -h argument on the command line.
impact: None in the current code for this vector. Historically, a host value carrying a semicolon or a command substitution would execute as an extra shell command on the operator's LAN host, and a value containing a slash could write outside the intended /dev/udp path prefix.
mitigation: Already fixed (setup/knock-lan.sh:141-149 and 166-177). Keep both layers - the whitelist and the positional-parameter form - and add a regression test asserting that the bash -c command string contains only the positional references and never the interpolated host/port values.
verification: Read setup/knock-lan.sh:130-200 and confirmed via git log -S 'P1-39' that the fix landed in commit 31509ea (2026-10-30). Verified the exact literal at setup/knock-lan.sh:171 contains "$1"/"$2" and not the interpolated host/port values. No script was executed and no file was modified.

title: Vendored acme.sh dns_huaweicloud.sh interpolates HUAWEICLOUD_Region into the DNS API host, but the panel never sets that variable so the candidate is not reachable
description:
ADJUDICATION RESULT: the candidate is real in the plugin but NOT reachable through the panel API. Recorded so the recon candidate is not re-raised.

Mechanism: the vendored plugin builds its API endpoint from an environment-controlled region label - _huaweicloud_region="${HUAWEICLOUD_Region:-ap-southeast-1}" and dns_api="https://dns.${_huaweicloud_region}.myhuaweicloud.com" (setup/vendor/acme-dnsapi/dns_huaweicloud.sh:41-42, repeated at :99-100). The region is interpolated into the HOST of the API URL, so a crafted value containing '@' or '/' would move the effective host - a value of 'x@evil.example/' would yield https://dns.x@evil.example/... , i.e. userinfo 'dns.x' with host evil.example.

Why it is NOT reachable: _acme_issue copies only the keys listed in the provider's STATIC fields array into the child environment (backend/app.py:12515-12516), and the huaweicloud entry of DNS_PROVIDERS declares ONLY HUAWEICLOUD_Username and HUAWEICLOUD_Password (backend/app.py:10178-10185). HUAWEICLOUD_Region is never set by any request path, so the plugin always falls back to its hard-coded default 'ap-southeast-1'. The only remaining exposure is the operator-controlled process environment (env = os.environ.copy(), backend/app.py:12514), which is not attacker-controllable.

REQUIRES: control of the panel process environment (operator-level), so this is LOW and is not an actionable finding as shipped.
impact: None through the panel API. A residual operator-controlled exposure only: if HUAWEICLOUD_Region were placed in the panel's process environment with a hostile value, the ACME DNS-01 flow for Huawei Cloud would talk to an attacker-chosen host instead of Huawei Cloud.
mitigation: No change is required for the panel. For defence in depth, validate HUAWEICLOUD_Region inside the plugin (reject anything outside ^[a-z0-9-]+$) before it is interpolated into the host, and add HUAWEICLOUD_Region to the provider field list as a validated enum if per-region selection is ever wanted.
verification: Read setup/vendor/acme-dnsapi/dns_huaweicloud.sh:41-42 and 99-100, backend/app.py:10178-10185 (the huaweicloud provider field list) and backend/app.py:12514-12516 (the env copy loop). Grepped backend/ for HUAWEICLOUD to confirm no other writer. No request was sent and no file was modified.

title: Reverse-proxy rule connectivity test leaks a three-state TCP port-scan oracle because the minimum-wait padding is skipped when the connect times out
description:
MECHANISM (verified line by line; no request was executed).

Entry: POST /api/reverse-proxy/rules/<rule_id>/test (backend/app.py:13341).

Sink: the handler takes the STORED rule's target_address (backend/app.py:13351), splits host:port (backend/app.py:13356-13360) and opens a raw TCP connection with no destination policy at all: sock = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_STREAM); sock.settimeout(5); sock.connect((host, port)) (backend/app.py:13387-13389). The only validation of target_address happens at rule-creation time in _validate_rp_service (backend/app.py:9968-9995) and is a FORMAT check only (_valid_upstream_host at backend/app.py:11431-11445, _sanitize_target_address at backend/app.py:9826-9853) - loopback, link-local and metadata addresses are accepted. Hostnames are resolved by the kernel at CONNECT time, so a name answering 127.0.0.1 or 169.254.169.254 on the second lookup gives a rebinding pivot.

Defect in the existing mitigation: the developers added a 1500 ms minimum-wait floor specifically to flatten the timing side channel (the rationale is spelled out at backend/app.py:13376-13382), but the padding is applied on only one branch. _wait = _RP_TEST_MIN_WAIT_MS - elapsed_ms (backend/app.py:13404) is followed by if _wait > 0: time.sleep(_wait / 1000.0) (backend/app.py:13405-13406). In the timeout case elapsed_ms is about 5000, so _wait is negative, no sleep happens, and the handler returns after the full 5 s socket timeout. The reachable case returns in about 1 ms and reports response_time_ms as the real measured elapsed time (backend/app.py:13398-13400). The three outcomes therefore remain distinguishable by response time: open about 1 ms, refused about 1500 ms, filtered/timed-out about 5000 ms. The response body distinguishes open from closed directly via target_reachable (backend/app.py:13414-13416).

REQUIRES AN EXISTING PANEL SESSION: the route is not exempt in before_request (backend/app.py:842-847). NO PRIVILEGE-BOUNDARY CROSSING IS CLAIMED - the same administrator can configure an arbitrary upstream target and reach it through the generated nginx rule - so this is recorded as a low-severity defence-in-depth defect in an implemented mitigation, not as an authorisation bypass. The developers' own comment at backend/app.py:13366-13374 already documents the oracle and the Shannon finding behind it.
impact: A holder of the panel session can turn the router into a LAN/loopback port scanner: probe any host:port reachable from the router and read a three-state result plus an audit line (backend/app.py:13411-13412). The mitigation that was written specifically to remove the timing oracle does not remove it.
mitigation: Pad from a fixed deadline rather than subtracting a floor. Compute the wait as max(0, DEADLINE - elapsed) where DEADLINE is the socket timeout (5 s), so that the refused case and the timeout case both return at the same 5 s boundary, and return a constant response_time_ms instead of the measured value (backend/app.py:13399). Alternatively, cap the socket timeout at the padding target so the timeout branch can never exceed it.
verification: Read backend/app.py:13341-13419 (the whole handler), 11431-11445 (_valid_upstream_host), 9826-9853 (_sanitize_target_address), 9968-9995 (rule-creation validation) and 795-872 (the auth interceptor). No request was sent to any device and no repository file was modified.

title: Unescaped client-controlled fields in the gateway nginx log_format let any client silently drop its own access-log lines from the visitor view (monitoring blind spot)
description:
The gateway nginx writes four client-controlled fields into a quoted, unescaped log format, and the panel's parser matches each of them with a quote-free character class, so a single double quote anywhere in those fields makes the whole access-log line fail to parse and disappear from the visitor view.

CHAIN:
(1) The log format is generated by the panel itself (backend/app.py:12082-12086):
    log_format nftgw '$time_iso8601 $remote_addr $request_method '
                    '$status $body_bytes_sent rt=$request_time '
                    'host="$host" uri="$uri" '
                    'ua="$http_user_agent" ref="$http_referer" '
                    'auth_user="$auth_user" auth_dev="$auth_device"';
nginx log_format has no escaping: $host, $uri, $http_user_agent and $http_referer are written byte-for-byte as the client sent them. A double quote is a legal VCHAR in an HTTP header value, so a User-Agent of x" reaches the log file unchanged.
(2) The parser (backend/app.py:8996-9002) is a single anchored regex; all six quoted fields are matched by [^"]* and the whole pattern is bounded by ^ and \s*$. An extra double quote inside a field terminates that field's [^"]* early, the following literal prefix ( ref=",  auth_user=", ...) no longer matches at that position, and because the pattern is anchored the engine cannot resynchronize on a later occurrence of the same prefix.
(3) The reader (backend/app.py:9034-9037) does m = _GW_ACCESS_RE.match(line.strip()) then if not m: continue - the line is discarded silently. There is no counter, no WARN, no unparsed field. _read_gateway_visitors is the only code in the tree that interprets the record format (the size probe at :9026 and the tail seek at :9029 belong to the same function); the only other code that touches the file is the size-capping cron script (backend/app.py:8916-8917, :8959), which copies raw bytes and never parses records. Nothing notices the loss - and the truncation script explicitly preserves the log tail for this very page (its own comment at :8950 says the tail is kept because the visitor page reads the most recent content), so the dropped records are gone from the panel's view of the retained history too.

The same defect applies to the auth_dev field, which is written from the RAW gw_device cookie on the public_access=false branch (auth_request_set $auth_device $cookie_gw_device;, backend/app.py:11765) and on the auth_lan_bypass branch of the authentication service (X-Auth-Device: request.cookies.get(COOKIE_DEVICE, ""), backend/auth_gateway.py:1975).

THREE SUB-QUESTIONS, EACH VERIFIED AGAINST THE EXACT COMPILED REGEX:
- Own line dropped: YES, CONFIRMED. A double quote in User-Agent or Referer (or in the request path, where nginx percent-decodes %22 into $uri) makes the client's own access-log line vanish from the visitor page - that IP loses those requests from its count, hosts, uris, statuses, ua and auth_dev.
- Forge another visitor's record: NOT POSSIBLE. The IP token is $remote_addr, the real TCP peer address, and it is the FIRST token of the line, before any client-controlled field, so no injection can reach it. The generated gateway config contains no set_real_ip_from / real_ip_header directive (grep over backend/app.py: the only X-Forwarded-For use is proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for at :11733, which does not affect $remote_addr). The IP therefore cannot be spoofed or forged through this path.
- Overflow into another field: NOT POSSIBLE. [^"]* cannot match a double quote, so a field's capture can never span a field boundary and absorb the next field's text. An injected quote only ever ADDS a token, while the regex demands exactly the six literal prefixes host= / uri= / ua= / ref= / auth_user= / auth_dev= in that order; any extra token desynchronizes the prefix sequence. The outcome is therefore always a dropped line, never a mis-parsed one (verified by exhaustive brute force, see verification).

Note the project's own audit path already knows this class of problem and fixes it: _sanitize() (backend/auth_gateway.py:1046-1055) strips control characters, with the comment that a newline in a UA lets you forge a whole login-success line in the remote log. That mitigation was never applied to the log_format / visitor path introduced with the 2026-11-18 visitor feature.
impact: Any unauthenticated external client of the public gateway port can make every one of its own requests invisible to the panel's visitor page by putting a single double quote in its User-Agent or Referer header. The attacker still appears in the gateway's own auth audit log (login_fail / verify_denied carry the real source IP, backend/auth_gateway.py:1849, :2153), and the raw nginx log file on the router keeps the line (the file itself is well formed), so the blind spot is confined to the visitor view and everything derived from it: the IP's visit count, the hosts / uris / statuses / UA shown to the administrator, and the who-has-been-touching-my-gateway triage view that the new visitor page exists to provide. Practical abuse is evading the administrator's investigation and the whitelist decision they would make from that screen. No firewall, authentication or whitelist decision reads this log, so there is no access-control bypass - severity is MEDIUM rather than HIGH.
mitigation: Fix the parser side, and make the loss visible. (a) Make the field captures resynchronize on the next literal prefix instead of aborting the line - e.g. ua="(?P<ua>.*?)"\s+ref=" - so an embedded quote no longer kills the record. (b) Count unmatched lines in backend/app.py:9035-9037 and surface the number next to the visitor payload (:9111-9118) or emit a WARN, so a silent drop can never again look like no traffic. (c) Write-side: nginx log_format offers no escape function, so the durable fix is to stop putting client-controlled values inside quotes in a fixed-prefix format (use a delimiter that cannot occur in the values, or log only server-controlled fields plus a correlation id). (d) Apply the same protection to auth_dev, which is written from the raw cookie on the public_access=false branch (backend/app.py:11765) and from the raw cookie in the LAN-bypass header (backend/auth_gateway.py:1975).
verification: Read backend/app.py:8991-9072 (format comment, _GW_ACCESS_RE, _read_gateway_visitors), :12082-12086 (log_format generation), :11560 (access_log directive), :11743-11765 (both auth_request_set branches), backend/auth_gateway.py:1963-2031 (_verify_or_deny) and :1046-1055 (_sanitize). Then executed the exact regex copied verbatim from backend/app.py:8996-9002 against synthesized log lines: clean line matches; one quote in ua / ref / uri / auth_dev -> no match; ua=x" ref="FORGED -> no match; ua=x" ip="1.2.3.4 -> no match; ua=x" auth_user="admin -> no match. Brute force over 729 crafted token combinations in ua x ref: 8 matched, and all 8 contained no quote at all - no injection produced a match. 20000 random UA strings: 15373 contained a quote, of which 0 matched and 15373 were dropped. Confirmed by grep that the generated gateway config has no set_real_ip_from / real_ip_header. No request was sent to 192.168.100.1 or .193; no repository file was modified (git status clean).

title: Client-asserted device id (gw_device cookie) and browser fingerprint (X-Device-Fingerprint header) are recorded as audit attributes without any verification, so device attribution in the audit log and in the visitor page can be impersonated
description:
Both device-identity signals used by the gateway are values the client asserts; the server narrows their charset but never proves them.

(1) DEVICE ID. device_id_from_request() (backend/auth_gateway.py:1518-1523) reads the gw_device cookie and accepts it as-is whenever it is 8-64 characters long and consists of [A-Za-z0-9_-]. Any client can therefore choose its own device id, including one identical to a legitimate user's. If the cookie is missing or malformed the function returns secrets.token_urlsafe(16) - a NEW random value on every call - so a client that simply omits the cookie gets a different device id on every single audit event (:1849 login_fail, :1945 logout, :2153 verify_denied). The value flows into the audit record (audit("login_ok", device=did, ...), :1902), into the token's dev claim (:516, :1900) and from there back out to nginx as the X-Auth-Device response header (:2005) and finally into the access log's auth_dev field (backend/app.py:12086).

(2) FINGERPRINT. fingerprint() (backend/auth_gateway.py:1526-1529) reads the X-Device-Fingerprint request header and returns it (truncated to 64 chars) whenever it matches [A-Za-z0-9_-]. The value is produced by browser JavaScript (backend/static/fingerprint.js:160 sends it) and is therefore entirely client-supplied; the server never checks that it is a hash, let alone the hash of the claimed device. It is only ever written to the audit log (:1763, :1849, :1863, :1902, :1945, :2153) - grep over backend/auth_gateway.py and backend/app.py finds no code that compares, counts or alerts on distinct fingerprints, so the anomaly detection advertised in backend/static/fingerprint.js:9 (spot the same account logging in from several unknown devices) is not implemented on the server side. The fingerprint is decorative.

(3) THE TWO NGINX BRANCHES DISAGREE ON SANITIZATION. The public branch takes the device id from the authentication service: auth_request_set $auth_device $upstream_http_x_auth_device; (backend/app.py:11749), and the token path returns a sanitized value (backend/auth_gateway.py:2005, str(payload.get("dev",""))[:64], where dev was minted from the charset-checked cookie and is HMAC-signed inside the token). The internal branch takes it straight from the cookie: auth_request_set $auth_device $cookie_gw_device; (backend/app.py:11765) - the RAW value, with no length or charset limit - and the authentication service's LAN-bypass branch does the same (X-Auth-Device: request.cookies.get(COOKIE_DEVICE, ""), backend/auth_gateway.py:1975). The same cookie therefore yields a sanitized identity on the token path and an arbitrary one on the two LAN paths.

CONSEQUENCE FOR AGGREGATION: the current code aggregates by IP, not by device (backend/app.py:9054), so aggregate-by-device is not yet implemented. But both attributes it would rely on are attacker-chosen: the auth_dev value the visitor endpoint returns (backend/app.py:9070-9071) and the device= field of the audit log are client-asserted. Any manual or future device-based correlation inherits the spoofability, and today's audit trail can already be poisoned - including by an unauthenticated attacker, who can put Cookie: gw_device=kirito-laptop on a wrong-password login and have the audit log record login_fail device=kirito-laptop.
impact: Device attribution in /var/log/nftables-web-auth.log and in its syslog mirror (backend/auth_gateway.py:1064-1076) cannot be trusted: an unauthenticated remote client picks the device id in the request, and a client that omits the cookie produces a fresh random device id per event, so per-device correlation of failed logins is impossible (the IP-based rate limit at :1848 still holds, so there is no brute-force amplification). The same raw value reaches the access log's auth_dev field on the two LAN branches, where it is neither length- nor charset-limited, and a double quote inside it additionally drops that client's own log line (see the log-format finding). No access-control decision consults the device id or the fingerprint - grep confirms every occurrence of dev is token payload, response header, cookie echo or audit field, and every occurrence of fingerprint() is an audit argument - so this is an integrity/attribution problem rather than an authentication bypass, hence MEDIUM.
mitigation: Mint the device id server-side and make it unforgeable: generate a random id when the client has none, persist it (or an HMAC of it keyed with the gateway secret) server-side, and accept only values the server itself issued. The token's dev claim is already HMAC-signed so it cannot be tampered with after login, but the pre-login gw_device cookie is fully client-chosen - that is the hole. Apply to the LAN branches the same sanitization the token path already has: stop using the raw $cookie_gw_device (backend/app.py:11765) and the raw cookie in the LAN-bypass header (backend/auth_gateway.py:1975); route both through one validating helper so the three branches cannot drift apart again. Treat the fingerprint as an untrusted hint: rename the audit field (e.g. fp_claim) or state that it is self-reported, and either implement the distinct-device check that backend/static/fingerprint.js:9 advertises or remove that claim from the documentation.
verification: Read backend/auth_gateway.py:203, :205, :509-526 (issue_token), :1046-1055 (_sanitize), :1064-1076 (_syslog), :1518-1529 (device_id_from_request / fingerprint), :1849, :1863, :1896-1902 (login path), :1945, :1963-2031 (_verify_or_deny: LAN bypass at :1975, token path at :2005), :2153; backend/app.py:11743-11765 (the two auth_request_set branches) and :12086 (the auth_dev log field); backend/static/fingerprint.js:9 and :160. Grepped backend/auth_gateway.py and backend/app.py for every use of the device claim (dev), of fingerprint(), and for distinct-device / known-device / new-device comparison logic: every dev occurrence is token payload, response header, cookie echo or audit field, and every fingerprint() occurrence is an audit argument - no decision depends on either value. Confirmed the charset check accepts any caller-chosen string (kirito-laptop is 12 chars of [A-Za-z0-9_-]) and that a missing cookie yields a fresh random id per call (secrets.token_urlsafe(16), :1523). No request was sent to 192.168.100.1 or .193; no repository file was modified (git status clean).

title: The gateway visitor endpoint is correctly restricted to panel sessions, but the requested observation window is silently not honoured - only the last 512 KiB of the access log is ever read while the API and the UI keep reporting the requested window
description:
ACCESS CONTROL OF THE NEW ENDPOINT IS SOUND: GET /api/gateway/visitors (backend/app.py:9075) is not covered by any exemption of the global before_request gate (backend/app.py:795-872). The exemptions are static assets (:834), / (:838), /api/auth/* (:842) and /api/knock-info (:846) - none of them matches /api/gateway/visitors, so the endpoint requires a valid panel session (panel_admin). The whitelist-promotion path it feeds, POST /api/lists/add (backend/app.py:8750-8823), sits behind the same gate and performs a live nft add element inet fw4 <set> (:8802). No anonymous caller reaches either.

THE DEFECT IS IN THE WINDOW ACCOUNTING. The parameter is clamped to 1..10080 minutes (backend/app.py:9083-9086, VISITOR_WINDOW_MAX_MIN at :9006) and echoed back to the client as window_minutes (:9116); the UI offers a 24-hour option (frontend/index.html:2367-2370). But the reader never scans the whole file: it takes only the last GATEWAY_LOG_TAIL_BYTES = 512 KiB of the access log (backend/app.py:9015, applied at :9026-9030) and then filters that slice by the cutoff (:9043). The access log lives on tmpfs and is only ever appended to (the comment at :9011-9013 says it only grows and never rotates); a size-capping cron script keeps the last 8 MiB once the file passes 20 MiB (LOG_TRUNCATE_MAX_BYTES / LOG_TRUNCATE_KEEP_BYTES, backend/app.py:8916-8917, applied by the script generated at :8959), and that script's own comment says the tail is preserved precisely for this page (:8950). Even with 8 MiB retained, the reader looks at 512 KiB of it, so once the log grows past 512 KiB the records for the requested window are present in the file but outside the slice the parser reads. A request for window=1440 then returns whatever fits in the last 512 KiB (on a busy gateway, minutes rather than a day) while the response still says window_minutes: 1440. Older records are silently absent and nothing in the payload reports the coverage that was actually read.

SECOND, SMALLER MISMATCH IN THE SAME AREA: total (:9115) is the number of distinct IPs found in the slice, while only the first VISITOR_MAX = 500 entries are returned (:9007, :9114). total can therefore exceed the number of rows rendered, with no truncated indication - the frontend binds rows with x-for over visitors.items (frontend/index.html:2407) and never learns that the table was cut.

This is a monitoring-accuracy defect, not an access-control one, hence LOW.
impact: On a gateway that has produced more than 512 KiB of access log inside the requested window (the log itself retains up to 8 MiB, so this is a parser limit rather than a storage limit), the administrator sees a visitor list far shorter than the window advertised (the UI still reads last 24 hours), so activity that has scrolled out of the tail - and any visitor it covered - is missing while the page claims full coverage. Combined with the log-injection blind spot (unescaped log_format, separate finding), the administrator can be shown a materially incomplete picture of who touched the public gateway, which is exactly the triage the visitor page was built for.
mitigation: Report the coverage that was actually read: capture the timestamp of the oldest line in the read slice (backend/app.py:9034-9043) and return it next to window_minutes (:9111-9118), then show it in the UI so a 24-hour claim is never made without the data to back it. Either size the tail to match the advertised maximum window (VISITOR_WINDOW_MAX_MIN = 10080 minutes, :9006; the log already retains 8 MiB, so 512 KiB is the only thing that has to grow) or cap the advertised window by what the log can actually provide, and note the tail cap in the endpoint docstring (:9011-9015) where the tail-is-enough assumption is made. Also add a truncated flag when total exceeds VISITOR_MAX so the administrator knows the table was cut.
verification: Read backend/app.py:8991-9119 (log format comment, _GW_ACCESS_RE, _read_gateway_visitors, the endpoint and its window clamp), :8906-8960 (the size-capping cron script and its constants), :795-872 (the before_request gate and its four exemptions), :8750-8823 (/api/lists/add, nft write at :8802), frontend/index.html:2345-2435 (visitor page: window options at :2367-2370, table rows at :2407-2426) and frontend/app.js:1513-1559 (loadVisitors at :1519, addVisitorToWhitelist posting the visitor row's IP verbatim to /api/lists/add at :1547). Confirmed by grep that /api/gateway/visitors appears in none of the before_request exemption branches. Not executed against a live log: the access log exists only on the device, and 192.168.100.193 was read-only for this task; the 512 KiB shortfall is derived from the code (tail constant vs. window parameter), not measured on a device.

title: POST /api/config/restore bypasses the config_rev optimistic-lock gate and silently rolls the live configuration back to the .backup snapshot
description: The whole-config write path enforces an optimistic lock, the restore path does not. POST /api/config computes the current revision from the snapshot it just loaded (app.py:2935 old_cfg = load_config(); app.py:2959 cur_rev = _config_rev(old_cfg)) and rejects a missing revision with 409 CONFIG_REV_REQUIRED (app.py:2960-2968) and a mismatched revision with 409 CONFIG_STALE (app.py:2969-2976). The comment at app.py:2938-2956 states the reason: a stale snapshot must never silently overwrite changes made by another device, tab or reverse-proxy write - that is exactly the 2026-10-21 .1 incident. POST /api/config/restore (app.py:3129) has no version parameter at all: it reads CONFIG_PATH + '.backup' (app.py:3132), json.loads it (app.py:3179-3180), inherits the live auth_token_epoch (app.py:3178, 3186), runs validate_config (app.py:3242) and then replaces the live configuration file wholesale with tmp + fsync + os.replace (app.py:3249-3254). The flock taken at app.py:3148-3149 only serialises concurrent writers against each other; it does not detect that the live configuration has moved on since the backup snapshot was taken. Consequently every configuration change made after the last successful save - a second browser tab, a reverse-proxy rule edit, a firewall/lan-members change - is discarded by one restore call, and the endpoint still answers {"success": true, "message": "配置已恢复，请刷新页面"}. Mitigations that ARE present on this path and must be credited: the epoch is inherited rather than restored (app.py:3178/3186 - an older epoch cannot be rolled back to re-activate revoked tokens), the restored content is validated before it lands (app.py:3242-3245), and the write is atomic (app.py:3248-3254). The gap is specifically the missing concurrency/version check.
impact: An authenticated panel administrator (or anyone holding a stolen panel session) can make the router silently fall back to an older firewall/policy configuration - trusted_ip4, lan_subnet4, port forwards, whitelist timeouts, knock ports - wiping out every change made since the last save, with no error and no diff shown to the operator. The loss is silent, which is the same failure mode the config_rev gate was introduced to stop. Precondition: a valid panel_admin session; no unauthenticated path to this endpoint exists (it is behind the global before_request gate at app.py:795-872).
mitigation: In restore_config() (app.py:3129-3266) apply the same optimistic lock as post_config(): require the caller to send the config_rev it believes is live and compare it with _config_rev(load_config()) before the replace, returning 409 CONFIG_STALE on mismatch (mirroring app.py:2957-2976). Because the backup is by definition older than the live file, the practical form is to store the revision alongside the backup when it is written (save_config, app.py:1379-1387) and refuse to restore a snapshot whose revision is newer than the live one, or at minimum require an explicit confirm=1 plus a returned diff of the fields that would be reverted.
verification: Read backend/app.py:2921-2976 (POST /api/config, the mandatory config_rev gate), app.py:3129-3266 (POST /api/config/restore - searched the whole handler for 'config_rev', '_config_rev' and any version comparison: none present), app.py:10828-10853 (_config_rev) and app.py:1319-1408 (save_config: flock + backup inside the lock). Grepped 'config_rev' over the whole of backend/app.py: the only occurrences are in post_config (2957-2976), _config_rev (10828-10853), the GET handler (2817-2818), preview-changes (3489-3492) and the READONLY key list (10805) - restore_config is absent from all of them. Static analysis only; no request was issued against any live device.

title: First-run setup is a TOCTOU race: POST /api/auth/setup only checks that the password file does not exist and _write_password_hash takes no lock, so two concurrent setups race and the last writer wins
description: auth_setup() (app.py:14153) guards itself with exactly one precondition: if _password_set(): return 400 ALREADY_SET (app.py:14169-14170). _password_set() is nothing but os.path.exists(AUTH_PASSWORD_FILE) (app.py:197-198) - a check and a later write with no lock between them. _write_password_hash() (app.py:210-218) acquires no lock and performs no exclusion: it opens the file with open(...,'w') and json.dump()s into it. Two concurrent setup requests therefore both pass the existence check (the file does not exist yet) and both write; the second write truncates and replaces the first, so the last writer's password is the one on disk. The session is established AFTER the write (app.py:14196-14203) and setup deliberately does NOT bump auth_token_epoch (compare auth_change_password, app.py:14235), so the loser of the race keeps a fully valid panel_admin session for a password that no longer exists - it can keep using the panel (its session cookie carries authenticated=True and the current epoch) while the password the operator believes was set is gone and the password the attacker chose is the live one. The setup endpoint is unauthenticated by design (first-run provisioning), so the winner of the race owns the appliance's single credential. Preconditions, all required: (a) the device is not yet initialised - the password file must not exist; (b) the requester must be inside the panel's allowed source nets - before_request applies _panel_allowed_networks() (app.py:826-830, fail-closed at app.py:606-715), and the /fw reverse-proxy path is NOT a way around it because nginx sets X-Real-IP to $remote_addr (app.py:11732) and _client_ip() trusts that header only from a loopback peer (app.py:2845-2856), so the panel sees the real client IP and rejects it with 403 IP_NOT_ALLOWED; (c) the attacker must win a narrow race window.
impact: An attacker who reaches the panel during the uninitialised window can end up owning the only credential of the appliance, and the legitimate operator is locked out of the password they just set (their session may still work, but they no longer know the password that is on disk). Rated LOW rather than MEDIUM because the endpoint is unauthenticated by design, it is restricted to sources inside the panel's allowed nets, and the window between the existence check and the write is short.
mitigation: Make the check-and-write atomic in _write_password_hash() (app.py:210-218): write the hash to a unique temp file, fsync it and os.replace() it into place, and create the final file with O_CREAT|O_EXCL so that exactly one caller can win the creation (the loser gets EEXIST and falls through to the ALREADY_SET branch). Alternatively take an exclusive flock on a dedicated lock file around the exists-check + write in auth_setup() (app.py:14169-14178), and bump auth_token_epoch after a successful setup so the losing session is invalidated.
verification: Read backend/app.py:14153-14204 (auth_setup), app.py:197-218 (_password_set / _read_password_hash / _write_password_hash - no flock, no O_EXCL, no tmp+replace), app.py:795-872 and 606-715 (the before_request gate and _panel_allowed_networks), app.py:2845-2856 (_client_ip) and 11732 (nginx sets X-Real-IP to $remote_addr, so the /fw path does not spoof the source). Grepped 'flock' across backend/app.py: the only flock users are save_config (1377), restore_config (3149) and the rate-limit table (455) - _write_password_hash is not among them. Static analysis only; no request was sent to any live device and no file was modified.

title: The panel password-hash file is written with truncate-then-write and no atomic rename, so a crash mid-write leaves a password file that exists but cannot be parsed - the panel can then never authenticate again
description: _write_password_hash() (app.py:210-218) creates the file with _ensure_file_mode(..., 0o640) and then writes with open(AUTH_PASSWORD_FILE, 'w') (app.py:214-215). 'w' truncates the file to zero length before the first byte of the new content is written, and json.dump() emits the object in several small write() calls; there is no temp file + os.replace(), no fsync and no lock. If the process is killed (OOM on a 1 GB device, a service restart) or the filesystem returns ENOSPC between the truncate and the last write, the file is left empty or half-written. The two consumers then disagree in the worst possible way: _password_set() only checks os.path.exists() (app.py:197-198) and therefore reports True, while _read_password_hash() swallows the JSONDecodeError and returns '' (app.py:201-207). The consequences are: auth_setup() refuses with ALREADY_SET (app.py:14169-14170) so the password can never be set again through the API, and auth_login() fails every attempt because _verify_password('', ...) is False (app.py:14129-14133). The panel's only credential-setting path is dead and the only recovery is out-of-band (SSH). The gateway, which reads the same file, fails closed (denies every login) rather than open, so this is an availability defect, not an authentication bypass. The identical truncate-then-write pattern in the same file is what the config writer explicitly avoids (save_config, app.py:1397-1403: tmp + fsync + os.replace).
impact: If the panel process dies or the disk fills during the write of a password hash, the appliance is left in a state where the password file exists but holds no usable hash: the administrator cannot log in and cannot re-run setup, and the appliance has to be recovered over SSH. The window is short (the payload is ~150 bytes) and the trigger is not attacker-controlled, hence LOW; the consequence is a denial of service against the appliance's only management interface.
mitigation: Rewrite _write_password_hash() (app.py:210-218) to the same pattern save_config() already uses (app.py:1397-1403): write the JSON to a unique temp file in the same directory, flush + os.fsync, chmod 0640, then os.replace() onto AUTH_PASSWORD_FILE - os.replace() is atomic, so readers see either the old file or the complete new one, never a truncated one. Additionally, make _password_set() validate the content (parse the JSON and check the 'hash' field is a non-empty pbkdf2_sha256$ string) instead of only testing existence, so a damaged file is reported as 'not set' and setup can be retried.
verification: Read backend/app.py:197-218 (_password_set / _read_password_hash / _write_password_hash) and compared with the atomic writer used for the configuration file (app.py:1397-1403). Read app.py:14153-14204 (auth_setup) and app.py:14110-14144 (auth_login) for the two consumer paths. Grepped for 'O_EXCL', 'fsync' and 'os.replace' in backend/app.py: none of them appears inside _write_password_hash(). Static analysis only; the password file on any live device was not read or written.

title: No CSRF token exists anywhere in the product; the only defences are SameSite=Lax cookies and a gateway-only Origin/Referer check on POST /auth/login, which leaves same-site cross-origin requests (sibling subdomains) able to force a gateway logout and a token rotation
description: Grep for 'csrf' / 'X-CSRF' over the whole of backend/ returns only the gateway's Origin/Referer check on POST /auth/login (auth_gateway.py:1784-1797) - there is no CSRF token anywhere in the product, on either service. The session cookies carry SameSite=Lax (panel: app.py:173 SESSION_COOKIE_SAMESITE='Lax'; gateway: auth_gateway.py:2452-2464, samesite='Lax' on gw_token and gw_device). What Lax actually blocks was verified rather than assumed: (1) A classic cross-site POST from a different registrable domain is NOT possible - the cookie is not attached, so POST /api/auth/change-password returns 401 at app.py:14217-14218 (the endpoint is inside the '/api/auth/' gate exemption at app.py:842-843 and re-implements its own check at app.py:14217) and POST /auth/logout cannot revoke anything, because _extract_token() (auth_gateway.py:1910-1936) finds neither a Bearer header nor a cookie and the handler returns 200 with nothing revoked (auth_gateway.py:1939-1944). (2) Lax does NOT block same-site cross-origin requests: 'site' for SameSite is the registrable domain, so a sibling subdomain of the operator's base domain is same-site and its cross-origin POST/GET still carries the cookie. This is not a hypothetical topology here - the gateway issues gw_token with Domain=<base domain> whenever the request host is under it (auth_gateway.py:2384-2412 _effective_cookie_domain, used at 2450/2461), which is the normal shape of a gateway that fronts several services by domain. From such a sibling, POST /auth/logout revokes the victim's gateway token (the endpoint requires no credential at all) and GET /auth/status forces a token rotation (auth_gateway.py:1652-1764). (3) Lax also does not block a cross-site top-level GET navigation, so the state-changing GET vector was checked: an AST analysis of all 31 pure-GET panel routes shows that none of them reaches a write (no save_config, no subprocess mutation, no file write in any GET handler), so that vector has no target on the panel. The panel's change-password is the least interesting target because it also requires old_password (app.py:14226); a same-site sibling attacker who does not know it only reaches _record_login_failure() for the victim's IP (app.py:14228), and five such requests lock the victim's own IP out of the panel login for 15 minutes (app.py:404-424). Finally, the recon's claim that GET /auth/status lets an attacker page 'force the victim's token rotation' is technically true but materially harmless, and is deliberately not rated as a vulnerability here: the replacement token is delivered only to the victim's own browser via Set-Cookie (auth_gateway.py:1762), the superseded jti is revoked (a mitigation, not a harm), and the project emits no Access-Control-* header anywhere (grep confirmed), so a cross-site page cannot read the response.
impact: From a sibling host under the operator's own base domain (typically one of the services the gateway fronts, or anything else able to serve content on that domain), an attacker page can terminate the victim's gateway session (POST /auth/logout revokes gw_token without needing any credential) and can force repeated gw_token rotations, and can burn the victim's own panel login-failure budget so that the victim is locked out of the panel for 15 minutes. No token theft, no credential disclosure and no cross-site POST against the panel is possible, because SameSite=Lax blocks the cross-site POST. Preconditions: the operator must be serving the gateway (or the panel through the /fw prefix) on a domain with at least one sibling host that an attacker can place content on; the victim must be logged in; no administrator credential is required.
mitigation: Add a double-submit CSRF token to the panel's mutating endpoints and to the gateway's POST /auth/logout: issue a random token in a readable (non-HttpOnly) cookie or in the session body, require the same value in a request header or form field, and compare it with hmac.compare_digest. In the panel, the natural place is the global before_request hook (app.py:795-872), which already exempts '/api/auth/' (app.py:842-843) - the exemption should carry the same CSRF requirement for change-password/setup/login instead of exempting the path outright. In the gateway, POST /auth/logout (auth_gateway.py:1939) should require the Origin check that POST /auth/login already performs (auth_gateway.py:1784-1797), and the gateway should stop raising the cookie to the parent domain (_effective_cookie_domain, auth_gateway.py:2384-2412) unless cross-subdomain sharing is explicitly required.
verification: Grepped 'csrf|CSRF|X-CSRF' over backend/ - the only hits are auth_gateway.py:1016, 1023, 1771-1797 (the login Origin/Referer check and its audit event) and app.py:173 / auth_gateway.py:2444-2464 (SameSite=Lax). Grepped 'Access-Control|CORS' over backend/ - only two comment lines, no response header is ever set. Read backend/app.py:795-872 (gate + exemptions), 14147-14253 (logout / change-password), 404-424 (login failure limiter) and backend/auth_gateway.py:1652-1764, 1784-1797, 1910-1960, 2384-2465. Ran an AST analysis over backend/app.py that enumerated all 84 routes, isolated the 31 pure-GET handlers and resolved their transitive call graph against a set of real write primitives (os.replace/chmod/remove/write, shutil.copy, subprocess.run, save_config, _mutate_lists, ...) - no pure-GET handler reaches a write, so no state-changing GET exists on the panel. Static analysis only; no cross-site request was issued and no live device was contacted.

title: The panel's login-failure rate-limit table fails open silently: a corrupt or unreadable table is swallowed into an empty dict with no warning, wiping every lockout
description: The panel keeps its login-failure counters in a JSON file (PANEL_RATELIMIT_FILE, app.py:340-342), written atomically with tmp + fsync + os.replace (app.py:364-375) and mutated under an exclusive flock (app.py:443-487). The read path, however, swallows every error: _ratelimit_read() catches (FileNotFoundError, json.JSONDecodeError, ValueError, OSError) and returns {} (app.py:354-361). Because the exception is consumed inside the reader, the caller's degrade path never runs: _check_rate_limit() calls _ratelimit_state(ip) inside a try that only catches OSError (app.py:409-413), so a JSONDecodeError never reaches _ratelimit_degrade(), no '[WARNING] 登录限流落盘不可用' line is ever printed, and st is None, which returns (True, None) = allowed (app.py:414-415). The effect is that a truncated, empty or otherwise unreadable rate-limit file silently disables the panel's entire brute-force protection - 5 failures per 5 minutes then a 15-minute lock (app.py:47-50, 404-424) - with no operator-visible signal whatsoever. The gateway has the same fail-open design but at least states it: _ratelimit_degrade() prints a warning and writes a 'ratelimit_degraded' audit record (auth_gateway.py:758-784), and the truncate-window reader defect was fixed by taking LOCK_SH (auth_gateway.py:2193). The panel's reader takes no lock at all and has no degradation notice. Since the file is written atomically the corruption trigger is not attacker-controlled (it needs write access to /etc/nftables, i.e. root), which is why this is rated LOW rather than MEDIUM: it is a silent-failure defence-in-depth defect, not an exploitable bypass.
impact: If the panel's rate-limit file is ever truncated, emptied or otherwise unparsable, the panel's login lockout silently stops working and the operator gets no warning: an attacker who can guess the password (or a legitimate operator who mistypes it five times) is never locked out, and there is no log line or UI state that says so. The blast radius is limited to the panel's own login endpoint (the public edge is the gateway, which has its own table and its own audited degradation path).
mitigation: Make the failure visible and keep the reader consistent with the writer: in _ratelimit_read() (app.py:354-361) distinguish 'file does not exist' (first run, legitimately empty) from 'file exists but cannot be parsed', and on the latter call _ratelimit_degrade() (app.py:378-386) and/or raise so that _check_rate_limit() (app.py:404-424) can decide the policy explicitly instead of inheriting an accidental fail-open. Take a LOCK_SH on the file in the reader, matching the writer's LOCK_EX in _ratelimit_mutate() (app.py:455), so a read can never observe a torn file.
verification: Read backend/app.py:326-487 in full (constants, _ratelimit_read, _ratelimit_write, _ratelimit_degrade, _ratelimit_state, _check_rate_limit, _record_login_failure, _clear_login_failures, _ratelimit_mutate) and compared with the gateway's equivalent (backend/auth_gateway.py:758-784, 868-978, 2161-2200). Confirmed by grep that _ratelimit_read is the only place where a JSONDecodeError can originate on the panel side and that it is swallowed there. Static analysis only; no rate-limit file was read or written.

title: The auth gateway's degraded-mode in-memory rate-limit fallback is read-modify-written without a mutex while the server is threaded, so concurrent failed logins can lose their counters and the 5-failure lockout never trips
description: The gateway's login limiter normally lives on disk under an exclusive flock (_mutate_ratelimit, auth_gateway.py:868-978). When that table cannot be opened or written - the case the module documents as having actually happened on .224, where /etc/nftables is not writable by the de-privileged uid nftweb (auth_gateway.py:758-778) - the limiter degrades to the in-process dict _RATE_FALLBACK (auth_gateway.py:755). That degraded path has no lock at all: _ratelimit_fallback_mutate() reads rec = _RATE_FALLBACK.get(ip), appends to rec['fails'], then assigns _RATE_FALLBACK[ip] = rec (auth_gateway.py:820-865), and _fallback_prune() mutates the same dict while iterating (auth_gateway.py:787-817); _ratelimit_fallback_is_locked() (auth_gateway.py:2161-2167) reads it unprotected too. The server is started with make_server(..., threaded=True) (auth_gateway.py:2665), so these dict operations genuinely interleave. Two concurrent failed logins can therefore read the same fails list, each append one timestamp and each write it back - one failure is lost. Repeating that loses enough counters that the 5-failures-per-5-minutes threshold (auth_gateway.py:745-747) never fires and the 15-minute lockout is never armed, which turns the limiter into a no-op exactly in the state where the disk path is broken. The same file protects its two sibling in-process tables with locks - _STATUS_RATE_LOCK for /auth/status (auth_gateway.py:751, used at 1637) and _AUDIT_RATE_LOCK for the audit table (auth_gateway.py:996) - the fallback table is the only one without one. The unbounded-growth half of this table was already fixed by _fallback_prune() (auth_gateway.py:787-817, RATE_FALLBACK_MAX_IPS eviction); the missing mutual exclusion is the remaining part.
impact: In the degraded state (rate-limit table missing or unwritable), an attacker sending parallel login attempts can lose failure counters and keep guessing the appliance password without ever being locked out; the victim (a real user mistyping a password) can also be denied the lockout that was supposed to protect them. The precondition is the degraded state itself, which the code documents as a real operational condition, so this is rated LOW rather than MEDIUM; the public edge rate limit is otherwise intact.
mitigation: Add a threading.Lock around the degraded table, mirroring the pattern already used twice in the same module: declare _RATE_FALLBACK_LOCK = threading.Lock() next to _RATE_FALLBACK (auth_gateway.py:755) and hold it across the whole read-modify-write in _ratelimit_fallback_mutate() (auth_gateway.py:820-865) and in _fallback_prune() (auth_gateway.py:787-817), and take it in _ratelimit_fallback_is_locked() (auth_gateway.py:2161-2167). A per-key lock, or simply reusing the same lock discipline as _STATUS_RATE_LOCK (auth_gateway.py:1637), is sufficient. Better still, make the degraded state loud enough that an operator restores the file instead of running with a weakened limiter.
verification: Read backend/auth_gateway.py:741-790 (constants, _RATE_FALLBACK, _ratelimit_degrade), auth_gateway.py:787-978 (_fallback_prune, _ratelimit_fallback_mutate, _mutate_ratelimit), auth_gateway.py:1626-1650 (_status_rate_ok and its _STATUS_RATE_LOCK), auth_gateway.py:2161-2200 (_ratelimit_fallback_is_locked, _is_locked) and auth_gateway.py:2660-2674 (make_server with threaded=True). Grepped for 'threading.Lock' in backend/auth_gateway.py: it appears only for _STATUS_RATE_LOCK (751) and _AUDIT_RATE_LOCK (996) - no lock guards _RATE_FALLBACK. Static analysis only; no login attempt was made against any live device.

title: POST /api/logd/config accepts any IPv4 as the remote syslog target with no destination allowlist, although the codebase has one for port forwards, and applying it restarts logd and wipes the local ring buffer
description: set_logd_config() validates log_ip only as a dotted quad whose octets are 0-255 (app.py:7910-7916); there is no ipaddress-based semantic check, so 127.0.0.1, 169.254.169.254, 0.0.0.0, 255.255.255.255 and any multicast address are all accepted, and the value is written straight into the system UCI section (app.py:7927+) and applied by restarting /etc/init.d/log, which forwards every syslog line - including the gateway's authentication audit records (source IP, User-Agent, device fingerprint) - to that address in plaintext (log_proto tcp/udp, port 1-65535, app.py:7918-7925). The same file already implements exactly the missing check for a different sink: _bad_forward_target() (app.py:1618-1632) rejects 127.0.0.0/8, 169.254.0.0/16, 0.0.0.0/::, broadcast and the router's own address for port-forward targets. Applying the logd change also restarts the logging daemon, which empties the local ring buffer - the code documents this at app.py:7868-7872 and reports it to the UI, so the operator is told, but the local forensic history is destroyed as a side effect of forwarding it elsewhere. Precondition: a valid panel_admin session; there is no path that reaches this endpoint without the global before_request gate (app.py:795-872).
impact: An authenticated panel administrator can point the device's syslog forwarder at an arbitrary IPv4 address, exporting all system and authentication logs (client IPs, User-Agents, device fingerprints, auth events) to a third party in clear text, and at the same time destroy the local ring buffer. Because the caller is already an administrator of a device on which it can run root commands, this is not a privilege-boundary crossing and is rated LOW; the finding is the missing destination allowlist and the inconsistency with _bad_forward_target().
mitigation: Reuse ipaddress-based semantic validation for log_ip in set_logd_config() (app.py:7910-7916): reject loopback, link-local (169.254.0.0/16), unspecified, multicast and broadcast addresses, i.e. the same classes _bad_forward_target() (app.py:1618-1632) already excludes for port forwards, and require the target to be a routable unicast address. Optionally require a second confirmation (the X-Confirm-Password step-up already used for certificate export, app.py:13646-13676) before the change is applied, since it both exports data and destroys the local buffer.
verification: Read backend/app.py:7836-7960 (get_logd_config / set_logd_config, the whole validation block) and app.py:1618-1660 (_bad_forward_target) and app.py:795-872 (the global session gate). Confirmed there is no ipaddress import/use in the log_ip validation path and no allowlist of any kind. Static analysis only; no configuration was read or written and no request was issued.

title: Recon claim not reproducible: a non-numeric ?limit= on GET /api/lists/history does not raise an uncaught ValueError (the int() conversion is wrapped), and neither service leaks a stack trace on an unhandled exception
description: The recon report states for GET /api/lists/history that 'int() in try/except, clamped 1..100' and, in the same bullet, 'a non-numeric value raises an uncaught ValueError -> 500'. The second claim does not hold in the current source: the conversion is wrapped - try: limit = int(request.args.get('limit', 20)) except (TypeError, ValueError): limit = 20 (app.py:9308-9311), followed by limit = max(1, min(limit, 100)) (app.py:9312). The other two integer query parameters are equally safe: GET /api/system/logs uses Flask's own converter, request.args.get('lines', 20000, type=int), which returns the default when the value cannot be converted, and the result is clamped to 1..20000 (app.py:7735-7736); GET /api/gateway/visitors wraps its int() in try/except and clamps to 1..VISITOR_WINDOW_MAX_MIN (app.py:9083-9086). An AST sweep of all 84 panel routes confirmed these are the only three integer conversions of request-supplied values. The second half of the claim - that a 500 would leak a stack trace - also does not hold: the panel registers only three specific error handlers (app.py:1290 ConfigCorruptedError, app.py:1304 ConfigWriteError, app.py:10603 DnsCredentialsStoreError), never a generic Exception handler, and the debug flag is never enabled - the FLASK_DEBUG-derived local at app.py:15522 is computed and then never used, because the server is created with make_server() (app.py:15524) rather than app.run(), so app.debug stays False and Werkzeug returns its generic 500 page without a traceback (the traceback goes to the server log, not to the client). The gateway is stricter still: it has an explicit catch-all @app.errorhandler(Exception) that returns a generic {'success': False, 'code': 'INTERNAL', 'message': '服务内部错误'} (auth_gateway.py:2468-2489). Conclusion: this recon candidate does not exist in the current code.
impact: None - the candidate is not reproducible. Recorded so that the reconciliation against the 10-29 baseline can mark it as already fixed rather than outstanding.
mitigation: No code change required. Keep the existing try/except around the int() conversions (app.py:9308-9311, 9083-9086) and keep the panel's debug flag unset; if the team wants belt-and-braces, add a generic @app.errorhandler(Exception) to the panel that mirrors the gateway's generic handler (auth_gateway.py:2468-2489), so that any future unhandled exception still returns a stable JSON error code instead of Werkzeug's default HTML page.
verification: Read backend/app.py:9304-9318 (list_get_history - try/except present), app.py:7720-7736 (get_system_logs - type=int plus 1..20000 clamp), app.py:9076-9086 (get_gateway_visitors), app.py:1288-1310 and 10600-10610 (the only three error handlers), app.py:15518-15530 (debug flag computed but unused; make_server with threaded=True) and backend/auth_gateway.py:2468-2489 (generic handler). Ran an AST script over backend/app.py that extracted every route decorator and every request.args/int() usage inside route handlers; the three parameters above are the complete set. Grepped 'app.debug|DEBUG|PROPAGATE_EXCEPTIONS|TRAP_HTTP' over both files: the only hit is app.py:15522. Static analysis only; no request was sent to any live device.

title: Verified, not a vulnerability: the operational endpoints really do write root scripts, rewrite /etc/config/network and restart networking, but every path is a hard-coded constant, every write is atomic and validated with rollback, and all of them are behind the panel session gate
description: This entry records the verification result for recon candidates AUTHZ-CAND-17 and AUTHZ-CAND-18 rather than a new vulnerability. The factual claims are all confirmed: POST /api/firewall/repair-init copies a hard-coded init script to /etc/init.d/nftables-web, chmods it 0755 and enables it (app.py:4762-4777); POST /api/firewall/install-china-ips writes the constant CHINA_IPS_SCRIPT to /opt/nftables-web-v2/update-china-ips.sh, chmods it 0755, adds a constant cron line to the root crontab and executes the script as root (app.py:5969-6020); POST /api/network/install-ipv6-cron writes the constant IPV6_CRON_SCRIPT to IPV6_SCRIPT_PATH (/opt/nftables-web/update-ipv6.sh, app.py:5018-5020) and upserts a constant cron entry (app.py:5747-5766); POST /api/network/lan-members rewrites /etc/config/network's bridge port list (app.py:4484-4610); POST /api/network/restart runs /etc/init.d/network restart and then re-applies the ruleset (app.py:4613-4658). What does NOT hold is the report's implied vulnerability. (a) No user-controlled string reaches a path: every destination is a module constant or an environment variable, and the cron lines are literals, so there is no path concatenation or traversal. (b) The crontab read-modify-write is fail-closed: a failed 'crontab -l' aborts the write instead of treating the crontab as empty (app.py:5995-5998 and _upsert_cron_for, app.py:5045-5048). (c) /etc/config/network is written atomically through _atomic_write_network_config() (app.py:4576) with a .backup copy (app.py:4568-4573), a semantic validator (_validate_network_config_content, app.py:4561) and a read-back check that rolls the file back on mismatch (app.py:4582-4599); member names must be existing physical interfaces, must not be reserved by WAN/other interfaces and the list may not be empty (app.py:4501-4555). (d) All five endpoints sit behind the single global session gate (app.py:795-872): no administrator-free path to any of them exists. The remaining risk is operator misconfiguration (e.g. moving the WAN port into the LAN bridge), which the code explicitly validates against and reports. Conclusion: as designed and as implemented these are administrator-initiated, root-level maintenance operations, not a privilege-boundary crossing, so no vulnerability is reported for them.
impact: None beyond what an authenticated administrator can already do. Recorded to close out recon candidates AUTHZ-CAND-17 / AUTHZ-CAND-18 with a source-level verdict and to keep the evidence in this file.
mitigation: No code change required for the paths themselves. Two optional hardening items, both already consistent with the codebase's own style: (1) /api/firewall/repair-init (app.py:4767) copies from /opt/nftables-web-v2/backend/nftables-web.init, a path outside the deployed package root used elsewhere (/opt/nftables-web/...), so it will silently 400 on a device deployed under the other prefix - align the constant with the deployment layout. (2) Consider requiring the X-Confirm-Password step-up (as used for certificate export, app.py:13646-13676) for /api/network/lan-members and /api/network/restart, the two endpoints whose failure mode is device lockout.
verification: Read backend/app.py:4762-4777 (repair-init), 5747-5766 + 5015-5061 (install-ipv6-cron and _upsert_cron_for), 5969-6020 (install-china-ips), 4484-4610 (save_lan_members, including _is_physical_iface / reserved-device / empty-list checks, the backup, the atomic write and the read-back rollback), 4613-4658 (restart_network), 795-872 (the global gate) and 1618-1660 (_bad_forward_target, for contrast). Searched the whole of backend/app.py for request parameters being concatenated into file paths in these handlers: there are none - every path is a constant or an env-var-derived module constant. Static analysis only; no endpoint was called and no file was modified.
